---
title: "Dynamic GxE from scratch"
subtitle: "Learning the daily growth rule of a crop from data, step by step, in R"
---

::: lead
A crop does not jump to its final yield; it grows a little every day, and how much it grows depends on that day's weather and on the genotype. This workshop shows how to **learn that daily growth rule from data**, using nothing but base R and a few lines per step.
:::

## The question we follow

> Can we learn the daily growth rule of wheat from simulated field trials, and use it to predict a **year the model has never seen**?

We work with one site (Narrabri), 199 wheat genotypes and 31 years of daily data from the public APSIM wheat simulations. The method is **SINDy** (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics): write the growth rate as a combination of a few candidate functions of the weather, and let the data decide which ones matter.

## The pipeline

Every step is a small function with a clear input and output. Any step can be replaced without touching the others, for example a different fitting method or a different library of candidate functions.

<table class="pipeline">
<tr><td><a href="01-idea.html">1 · The idea</a></td><td>A model of change is a running total of daily growth. A toy example, solved with <code>lm</code>.</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="02-data.html">2 · The data</a></td><td>Two plain tables: daily weather and daily biomass.</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="03-design.html">3 · Library and design matrix</a></td><td>Candidate functions of the weather, stacked into a regression problem.</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="04-fitting.html">4 · Fitting</a></td><td>OLS, ridge and sparse regression, all behind one signature.</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="05-validate.html">5 · Simulate and validate</a></td><td>Roll the equation forward and test it on held-out years.</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="06-reading.html">6 · Reading the model</a></td><td>Response curves: what the equation says about weather and growth.</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="07-genotypes.html">7 · Genotypes</a></td><td>A shared model plus genotype deviations, and ranking lines.</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="08-pitfalls.html">8 · When it breaks</a></td><td>Wrong libraries, collinear drivers, one-step versus rollout fit.</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="09-further.html">9 · Going further</a></td><td>Adding crop knowledge, coupled states, and the Bayesian version.</td></tr>
</table>

## How to follow along

Every page runs on its own and takes seconds. The whole pipeline, including leave-one-year-out cross-validation over all 199 genotypes, runs in about ten seconds.

```r
# base R is enough; ggplot2 is only used for the plots
install.packages("ggplot2")
source("R/functions.R")      # all modelling functions, plain base R
```

Start at [Set up](setup.html), or jump straight to [the idea](01-idea.html).

::: {.callout-note title="Where the data come from"}
The data are simulated biomass and daily weather for four Australian sites, from Bustos-Korts et al. (2019), *From QTLs to adaptation landscapes: using genotype-to-phenotype models to characterize G×E over time*, Frontiers in Plant Science 10:1540. Because the data are simulated, the true crop parameters are known, which lets us check what the method recovers.
:::
